clue.text: John seizes the luggage space as a sign of aggression

parts.note: Jack is a familiar form of the name John
the boot is a British car's luggage compartment

explanation.surface: A man commandeering the car's boot is behaving aggressively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seizes' is only a link here, joining JACK to BOOT; BOOT is the British word for a car's trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavy military jackboot is a symbol of bullying, authoritarian force.

clue.text: Edward, gent at heart, in paradise

parts.note: Ed is a short form of Edward

indicators.note: at heart points to the middle letters of the word gent

explanation.surface: Edward, a gentleman at heart, is blissfully happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at heart' takes EN, the middle of GENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden of Eden is the biblical paradise, so the name serves as a synonym.

clue.text: Is it in the "Gardeners' Year Book"?

definitions.text: Is it in the "Gardeners' Year Book"?

parts.words: Is it in the "Gardeners' Year Book"?
parts.note: two senses meet: a yearly book is one kind, and a plant lasting one growing season is another, which a gardeners' book would list

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a book published every year and a plant that completes its life in one season.

clue.text: Died with snow all around — a drawback

indicators.note: all around suggests the letters of died and snow are scattered about and remixed

explanation.surface: Someone perished in a blizzard, which was certainly a disadvantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all around' looks like a description of the snow, but it is the anagram signal for both words; 'with' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: A downside is a disadvantage or negative aspect, the same as a drawback.

clue.text: American poet, verbose guy

parts.note: long-winded or long describes verbose speech
fellow is another word for a guy or man

explanation.surface: An American poet described as a long-winded chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was a nineteenth-century American poet, author of Hiawatha.

clue.text: Might he fiddle with a corset?

definitions.text: Might he fiddle with a corset?

indicators.note: to fiddle with something is to mess it about, so the letters of corset get rearranged

explanation.surface: A suggestive question about a man toying with a lady's corset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddle with' rearranges CORSET; the whole clue also describes a male companion getting too familiar.
explanation.definitionFit: A male escort, a paid companion, is the kind of man the whole clue imagines fumbling at underwear.

clue.text: This shrub needs well-constructed drainage

indicators.note: well-constructed implies the letters of drainage are built into a new shape

explanation.surface: A gardening tip that a certain bush requires good soil drainage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-constructed' rearranges DRAINAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: The gardenia is an evergreen flowering shrub with fragrant white blooms.

clue.text: "The true one will let his wife starve", having bad traits

definitions.text: "The true one will let his wife starve"

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters of traits are in a poor, disordered state

explanation.surface: A cynical quotation about devoted creatives neglecting their families, linked to bad character traits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges TRAITS. The definition quotes Shaw's Man and Superman: the true artist will let his wife starve.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw wrote that the true creative person lets his wife starve rather than compromise his work.

clue.text: Player's boot is undone

indicators.note: something undone has come apart, so the letters of boot is are loosened and rearranged

explanation.surface: A footballer's bootlace has come untied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undone' rearranges BOOT IS; the 's of Player's is just 'is' linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An oboist is a musician who plays the oboe, so a kind of player.

clue.text: Just a crust for son and family

parts.note: kin means one's family or relatives

explanation.surface: Nothing but a crust of bread to share between a boy and his relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' just joins definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin is a thin outer layer or coating, much as a crust is on bread or custard.

clue.text: West Ham's park — nothing accomplished. Doing something wrong?

parts.note: Upton Park was the long-time home ground of West Ham United football club
O looks like zero, nothing
good can mean skilled or accomplished

explanation.surface: A sorry report that the football club's ground has achieved nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Upton Park in east London was West Ham United's football stadium until 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: To be up to no good is the idiom for being engaged in mischief or wrongdoing.

clue.text: Inspector takes on learner driver in scrap

parts.note: Inspector Morse is the TV detective created by Colin Dexter
L is the plate displayed by a learner driver in Britain

explanation.surface: A police inspector agreeing to teach a driving student, in a fragment of a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a British TV detective; L-plates mark a learner driver in Britain. 'takes on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece or scrap, especially of food.

clue.text: Tread on large snake and it will lift you up

parts.note: a step is the tread of a stair
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
the adder is a venomous snake

explanation.surface: A warning that stepping on a big snake will make you leap.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has you jump in fright; the definition is a literal piece of equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepladder is a folding ladder used to raise a person up to reach high places.

clue.text: Shoe seen in messy toilet behind street

indicators.note: behind puts the jumbled word after the abbreviation for street
messy suggests the letters of toilet are in disarray

explanation.surface: A woman's shoe spotted in a dirty public loo at the back of the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'messy' rearranges TOILET into ILETTO, placed 'behind' ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a woman's shoe with a high, thin heel.

clue.text: It's an effort to go round Waterloo with it

indicators.note: to go round means the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: a try is an attempt or effort
meeting one's Waterloo means one's final defeat, so Waterloo stands for the end

explanation.surface: Travelling around a London station takes some effort, even for a fashionable person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go round' is the container signal. Waterloo stands for a finish via the idiom 'to meet one's Waterloo', a final defeat; the surface suggests the London station.
explanation.definitionFit: Being with it is slang for being fashionable or up to date.

clue.text: Grand old ladies make bets

parts.note: do can mean make, as in do a meal
wagers are bets

explanation.surface: Elderly aristocratic women having a flutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make bets' reads as DO WAGERS, run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Dowagers are dignified elderly women, especially widows holding a title from a late husband.

clue.text: Family keeps nearly everything secured

indicators.note: keeps means the first word holds another inside it

parts.note: seed means offspring or descendants, a family line

indicators.note: nearly means one letter is dropped from the end

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: A household that hangs on to almost everything it owns has it locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' trims the word for everything by its last letter, and 'keeps' puts what remains inside the word for family.
explanation.definitionFit: Sealed means closed up tight, firmly secured against opening.

clue.text: Dry? I must get soda mixed for a film star

indicators.note: mixed implies the letters of the preceding words are blended together

explanation.surface: A teetotal starlet insists on a soda to settle her thirst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' rearranges DRY, I and SODA.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris Day was a popular American actress and singer of 1950s Hollywood films.

clue.text: I'd better keep Isle of Man's expressions

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
IOM is the abbreviation for the Isle of Man, with the 's giving S

explanation.surface: Someone resolves they ought to retain the Manx island's sayings.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is a self-governing island between Britain and Ireland, abbreviated IOM. 'better keep' only joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning is not literal.

clue.text: Love and marry behind the lobby, which is sacred

indicators.note: behind means these pieces come after the lobby

parts.note: a hall is an entrance lobby
love is zero in tennis, written O
to wed is to marry

explanation.surface: Romance and a wedding held in a vestibule of a holy building.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is a nil score in tennis; 'behind' places the love-and-marry pieces after the lobby.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallowed means made holy or consecrated, which is to say sacred.

clue.text: Open a Bible with love when getting hitched

parts.note: AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible
love is nil in tennis, written O
getting hitched is slang for marrying, to wed

explanation.surface: A couple open a Bible with affection at their wedding ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' looks like a verb to do with the Bible; it is the adjective, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Avowed means openly declared or acknowledged, so open in that sense.

clue.text: Baby needs company near hospital beds

parts.note: a ward is a room of beds in a hospital

explanation.surface: An infant needs other people around it close to the hospital beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby' is an insult for a fearful person, not an infant.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a baby means they are timid or cowardly.

clue.text: Withdraw and call elsewhere

parts.note: to cry is to call out
off can mean away or elsewhere

explanation.surface: Advice to back out and telephone another number.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry off is to back out of an arrangement, to withdraw.

clue.text: A smug person wants a doubly attractive thing

indicators.note: doubly means the word is given twice over

parts.note: a goody is something attractive or desirable, like a treat

explanation.surface: A self-satisfied person craves twice the treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubly' repeats GOODY.
explanation.definitionFit: A goody-goody is someone smugly virtuous and self-righteous.

clue.text: Some food is hot here

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner's remark that a portion of the meal is spicy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also points at the answer: the food is here, on the plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Read with the clue, the dish is where the hot food is, so 'here' points at the serving vessel.

clue.text: Tear drop

definitions.meaning: to tear is to rush or run quickly
a drop is a small splash of liquid added, as of milk

explanation.surface: A teardrop on someone's cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash means both a rush (to tear along) and a small amount (a dash of milk).

clue.text: There's nothing in the recorder but a streak of light

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a meter records readings, a recording device
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A measuring device that reads zero, yet a flash appears in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recorder' suggests the musical instrument; it is a measuring meter.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteor is a shooting star, seen as a brief streak of light across the sky.

clue.text: See a fast scramble to be an MP's banker

indicators.note: scramble means the letters of the preceding words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A parliamentary candidate rushes to bag a guaranteed constituency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scramble' rearranges SEE A FAST. A banker is British slang for a certainty; an MP is a Member of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: A safe seat is a constituency where an MP is almost certain to win, a sure thing or banker.
